title: Describe a time when your team missed a deadline: what happened, what was your role, and what did you do about it?
shortTitle: Team Missed a Deadline: what happened and what did you do?
keyPoints: Communicate the risk early before the deadline, not after.
Name the real root cause without blaming individuals: scope creep, underestimated dependency, unexpected incident.
Re-scope intelligently: ship the critical path on time and defer nice-to-haves.
Protect quality even under deadline pressure, especially for money-handling code.
Close with a durable process improvement so the same estimation miss does not repeat.
Take ownership of your part honestly rather than hiding behind the team.
Track planned versus actual progress visibly so slippage surfaces early.

s1_definition.oneliner: Missing a deadline is a fact; how early you communicate it and what you fix afterward is what defines you.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Early communication** – Raise the risk before the deadline, not after; silence until the last day is the worst response.
- **Honest root cause** – Name the real reason (scope creep, underestimated dependency) without blaming individuals.
- **Intelligent re-scoping** – Ship the critical path on time and defer less essential features to the next iteration.
- **Quality protection** – Never ship broken money-handling code to hit a date; a one-week delay beats a production incident.
- **Durable fix** – Change estimation or planning so the same miss does not repeat.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India promised a new statement-download feature for Priya's current account by month end, but the team slipped. Missing a deadline is like a bank branch promising a loan decision by Friday and not delivering. What matters is not that the delay happened, but whether you called the customer early, explained honestly, and made sure the next promise was realistic.

sections.s6_takeaway:
At National Bank of India, my team committed to deliver a transaction-search feature for customers like Rajesh and Priya within a two-week sprint. Halfway through, a dependency on our audit service turned out to be far more complex than estimated, and it became clear we would not finish everything on time. My role was to own the delivery honestly.

The first thing I did was make the slippage visible early. We tracked remaining work against an ideal burn-down line every day, and by day three it was obvious we were falling behind. Instead of staying quiet and hoping to catch up, I raised it immediately with my manager and stakeholders, explained the real root cause, and did not blame any individual.

Then I re-scoped intelligently. Rather than ship everything late or ship something half-tested on time, I proposed delivering the critical search path on the original date and deferring the advanced filters to the next sprint. We shipped the core feature on time and the rest a week later, with no quality compromise on the money-related paths.

The lasting fix was the most important part. We changed how we estimate work with external dependencies, adding a spike task to de-risk unknowns before committing to a date. After that, our estimates got far more accurate.

Remember one sentence: Detect slippage early, communicate it honestly before the deadline, re-scope to protect the critical path and quality, and fix the estimation process so it does not repeat.
